items.title: Mauricio Pochettino Leaves The USMNT For An Even Bigger Mess
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
After an extended denouement to a doomed tenure, Manchester United finally set manager Michael Carrick loose on Thursday, hoping to put an end to the club's worst league start in 40 years. On Friday, the next era for England's most famous club began, sort of, as United announced that Mauricio Pochettino would be leaving the U.S. men's national team on Nov. 18 in order to become the new boss at Old Trafford.

Carrick's departure is no surprise, but Pochettino's arrival counts as a bit of a shock. Pochettino had famously come to international prominence first at Southampton and then in his five-season-plus stint at Tottenham Hotspur, which saw that club's evolution from an also-ran into, well, an also-ran that could actually fight with the big boys. Eventually, his tenure there grew stale and the lack of trophies forced a move, with Tottenham firing him in November of 2019. The Argentine then took a year off before signing on to succeed Thomas Tuchel at Paris Saint-Germain in early 2021; his first half-season there wasn't great, as he oversaw the only PSG squad to not win the Ligue 1 title this decade. He did go on to win the league in his first full season, but PSG let him go in the summer of 2022 anyway. A return to the Premier League with Chelsea followed in 2023, where he finished in sixth place in his only season at Stamford Bridge.

That brings us to September 2024, when Pochettino became manager of the USMNT ahead of the 2026 World Cup cycle. His appointment was a big deal, as he became the highest-paid and most accomplished manager in the country's history (Jurgen Klinsmann will quibble with the latter assessment, but whatever) in advance of a home(-ish) World Cup. Pochettino had a rocky start there, but eventually righted the ship enough to guide the USMNT to a Group D first-place finish and a Round of 32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. An embarrassing loss to Belgium in the Round of 16 put a bit of a damper on the run, but overall, Pochettino did what he was hired to do: help the USMNT perform at the World Cup.

items.title: Utah’s Superhero Keeper Will Face Washington’s Attacking Horde
items.author: Abigail Segel
items.content:
Before the NWSL playoffs started, I predicted, like many, that San Diego would go all the way. The second-seeded Wave were so solid, so well-balanced, and with a possession-based style that steamrolled team after team. Making it past the faltering, Mina Tanaka–less Utah Royals in the quarterfinals didn't feel anything close to a question. Where San Diego had earned 25 points in the final 10 matches of the regular season, Utah earned just 11.

I've never been so happy to be wrong. In delivering a 1-0 upset in San Diego last Friday, Utah provided a postseason performance that left me, a neutral, pumping with joyful adrenaline. 

As expected, San Diego dominated in nearly every way: shots, possession, touches in the final third. But the only stat that matters is goals scored, and Utah goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn had something to say about this.

items.title: Notre Dame Brings Havoc To The CFP Rankings
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Lots of things got chucked in the bin last week: Miami's unbeaten season and Mario Cristobal's muffled rage, Ryan Day's offseason peace of mind, Lane Kiffin's shiny glow in Baton Rouge, the Heisman Trophy projections (now it's Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker and Boise State running back Dylan Riley as the favorites, right?), Nebraska's budget for the next seven years if it fires Matt Rhule and has to pay him $63 million to turn in his sideline credential—in all, it's just getting thicker at this end of the trough.

As a result, Georgia is the new badass in residence after stomping Ole Miss, 42-7, and UCLA and Utah are last unbeaten teams in FBS. Texas is back—what, for the third time now?—and there are still five Big Ten coaches who haven't gotten the memo to rip ESPN for jerry-rigging the committee rankings to satisfy their SEC overlords. Remember, children: A conspiracy doesn't have to be proven to be advanced—it only has to sound evil to be convincing—and college football's various hierarchies have been doing Satan's bidding since 1869. But never mind all that; you're already bought in, so enjoy hell. For now, let's dance that ska.

items.title: Soccer Can Find Salvation In A Bag Of Tricks
items.author: Aaron Timms
items.content:
The suspended rabona, the showy drag with the left foot, the ricochet off the defender, the bobble of instinctive control on the byline with the right, then back onto the left for a quick push with the outstep into the goalmouth, where a teammate applies the finishing touch.

Even a few weeks later, the rabona-croqueta that Lamine Yamal improvised in Barcelona’s recent Champions League win over Galatasaray astonishes with its ingenuity. Did he intend the move to come off exactly as it did? We don’t know. Does it matter? It does not.

items.title: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
It's just like they told you it would happen in D.A.R.E.: You have been miraculously, tragically transported 2,800 years back in time, in the land that is now the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. The site will be eventually called Tunnug 1 by the archaeologists who excavate it in 2017. But that is the future, and this is the present, meaning 800 B.C. You have come to sit with the Scythians, nomads who roamed the Eurasian steppes on horseback. You have even glimpsed their warrior-king, whose long and stately braids make him seem like a pretty cool guy. Also, he's smoking. Suddenly the warrior-king glimpses you back, his reddish eyes glinting in the firelight. He leans over to you, whispers something inscrutable in an Eastern Iranic language, and extends in his grizzled hands an ancient joint, leaving you with only one question: Would you smoke that shit?

There are, to be certain, pros and cons. But one thing is clear, per a paper published recently in the journal : The Scythians were definitely using cannabis to get high. The analysis, led by Fabio-haired University of Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari, represents the earliest definitive evidence of humans consuming marijuana as a psychoactive drug, which was previously only traced back 2,500 years ago where Sogdian mourners once lit up in the ancient Jirzankal Cemetery in what is now western China.

It's only fitting that marijuana hails from one of the highest places in the world: the eastern Tibetan Plateau, also known as the Roof of the World. The plant evolved around 28 million years ago, and as early as 4,000 years ago Chinese farmers cultivated the plant for rope, clothing, and paper, per But it is harder to tell when in the archaeological record ancient people first became gone off that loud. Wild weed, the ancestors of the domesticated kind, has only a little tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the plant's intoxicating compound. Some researchers confirmed this when they tried to smoke wild weed and felt nothing, also per . (It is unclear if these particular researchers are also the paper's authors, who described cannabis as an "illicit" substance.)

items.title: Horny Nvidia CEO No Longer CEO, Possibly Still Horny
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who is worth over $100 billion, resigned as CEO on Thursday morning, following an emergency board meeting prompted by several reports that he'd been having various affairs, most notably with someone U.S. officials believe was spying on behalf of the Chinese government.

Nvidia has an unorthodox corporate structure, built around Huang, which largely eschews traditional executive roles in favor of a large council of vice presidents who report directly to Huang, which makes the matter of his succession trickier to game out than it would be in other cases of a CEO doing sex stuff. He'll be succeeded on an interim basis by Colette Kress, formerly the CFO, whom characterizes as one of the few people with a high-level grasp of the company's finances and ties to Wall Street.

A quick recap of how we got here: Nvidia is the single most important hardware technology company in the world, a chip designer that boosted its market cap to more than $4 trillion by making the must-have picks and shovels of the ongoing AI boom. As such, Nvidia is something like a shadow arm of the U.S. government, the latter of which is engaged in the stupidest-ever version of the space race with China over who can build the machine god first. Nvidia wants to sell its best stuff to Chinese companies because it doesn't really care who wins, as long as it makes money for investors, but the Trump administration won't allow it. Meanwhile, the tip-top Chinese AI companies have found ways to smuggle in the best Nvidia chips via third parties mostly based in Southeast Asia.

items.title: How I Succumbed To Reef Madness And Came To Love A Slowly Sinking Ship
items.author: Dave McKenna
items.content:
The SS finally sank in the Gulf of Mexico at around 10 p.m. ET Wedneday night. Not since the had a doomed vessel’s last tour run so far over schedule and still kept viewers engaged. Those who stuck with the 10-hour livestream were rewarded with an amazingly touching denouement. 

The ship had its day. The SS hit the seas in 1952, and at 990 feet long was about 100 feet longer than the Titanic, yet was able to hit speeds of more than 38 knots, still faster than any transatlantic ocean liner ever. But it was deemed obsolete and taken out of service way back in 1969, and spent the last 30 years docked in Philadelphia. Attempts to keep the SS above water as a hotel or museum failed, and some folks in Okaloosa County, Florida, decided the liner was most valuable at the bottom of sea. The county floated a $10 million plan to turn the ship into an artificial reef and thereby enhance the Redneck Riviera’s reputation as a fishing and scuba diving destination. This entailed sinking the SS about 22 miles off Fort Walton Beach during the very same week that the hit bottom 51 years earlier.

Imagine how inept college officials must be by comparison. Conferences would probably be better off asking parents to do the job.

items.title: ‘Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life’ Is Dishy And Definitive
items.author: Max Pearl
items.content:
Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life might seem like a bland title for a biography, until it dawns on you exactly how much living the man did. He eloped with his aunt at 19, then humiliated her by writing a novel about it translated into more than 30 languages; divorced her for her much younger niece, his first cousin; and, after a scandalous 50-year marriage beset by separations, walked out one last time for the Spanish socialite and tabloid favorite Isabel Preysler, ex-wife of Julio Iglesias and mother of Enrique.

Arguably the world’s most famous Peruvian after Paddington, Vargas Llosa would have been president if not for the dark-horse populist Alberto Fujimori—father of the current president—who handily defeated Vargas Llosa’s platform of neoliberal shock economics in 1990. And in 2010, at age 74, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, joining the pantheon alongside his lifelong frenemy Gabriel García Márquez, whom he famously punched in the face at a film premiere, for reasons that remain unclear. 

Thus, the page count of the new biography—the first since his death in 2025 and almost certainly the last word on the subject—clocking in at 812. Gerald Martin, a British critic who also wrote the definitive book on García Márquez, spent 25 years interviewing Vargas Llosa and those who knew him. The result is a monumental achievement: a synthesis of his subject's personal and political life with a surgical yet shockingly breezy analysis of the writing itself. And while it’s not always right to conflate fictional characters with their creator, Vargas Llosa is a special case, Martin argues: a novelist who peppered his work with confessions.

items.title: New House Minority Leader Still Faces Old Questions On Ohio State Sexual Abuse
items.author: Diana Moskovitz
items.content:
Jordan previously ran for the role of Speaker of the House in 2023 but failed three times to get a majority of the votes needed. This too was voted on by secret ballot. At the time, those who did speak about their "no" votes told NPR they voted against Jordan because of bullying and threats being made to them and their families by either Jordan or Jordan supporters.

But at that time, Jordan also was continuing to face questions about his connection to Ohio State's sexual abuse scandal. In 2018, former wrestlers for the university came forward, saying they had been sexually abused by a team doctor under the guise of him providing them with medical treatment, usually during a physical exam. The wrestlers forced an independent investigation, and the ensuing published report said that Dr. Richard Strauss sexually abused "at least 177 male student-patients" at Ohio State, many of them while he worked in the athletics department from the late 1970s until 1998. Strauss died by suicide in 2005.

items.title: The Oilers Are A Bunch Of Squirts And A Couple Of Gods
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
For the second goal of the Oilers' 3-2 win over the Philadelphia Flyers, the NHL's best offense converted yet another power play. Zero points for guessing the man who picked up the primary assist: Connor McDavid now has a 15-dish lead over the next-highest guy on the league's assist leaderboard, as well as a 12-point lead in overall points. The next two guys on the latter list, by the way, are both Oilers, too.

With the score 1-0 in the second period, and Oliver Bonk serving a two-minute penalty for bonking (OK, fine, interference), McDavid captured the defense's attention by skating with the puck far out on the left in the attacking zone. In doing so, he was able to give his teammate Zach Hyman a little bit of personal space right in front of the crease. This is the part that he made look easy: He fired a quick centering pass through two alert Flyers and got the puck to an awkward spot right at goalie Dan Vladar's knees. Hyman just had to poke his stick around in there to encourage the biscuit over the line.

items.title: Why Do People Keep Cheating At Marathons?
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
When asked why he kept trying to climb Mt. Everest, the climber George Mallory famously replied, "Because it's there." When asked about his creative process, creator Will Wright said, "I don't know. I thought it would be cool." I've always been struck by the inscrutability of inspiration, by the notion that we can't always explain why we do the things we do. This week's episode of gets into this psychic terrain by way of examining the question of why so many people cheat at marathons.

The premise of the show is that cheating can most often be understood as a rational calculation. Someone chooses to break the rules because they ultimately decide that the benefit of getting away with it outweighs the downside of getting caught. But cutting the course on a marathon doesn't fit into this heuristic. Most marathon cheaters don't really cheat anything, at least not anything that matches up to the shame and derision that comes with being exposed as a cheater. This dynamic is especially true these days, when cheaters both are easier to catch and have less to gain. In late September, an influencer was caught hitching a ride on a bike at the Berlin Marathon en route to posting the unremarkable time of 4:53:46.

Taken as a whole, marathon cheating suggests that there's an unscratchable itch, a desire to break the rules for the simple sake of doing it. To break it all down, I drafted in our old friend Dennis Young, whom you may know from his time with us at the old site or for his current work editing Front Office Sports. Dennis is great, and we had a fun time getting into it.

items.title: Call Her Petty
items.author: Kelsey McKinney
items.content:
In the fall of 2018, Alexandra Cooper and Sofia Franklyn released the first episode of by introducing themselves. “To be honest, I’m probably here just to ride Alex’s coattails,” Franklyn said. Cooper, more confident on mic in sound and delivery, declares herself a “stay-at-home, try-hard vlogger by day and an Insta-hoe by night.” The show, which at the time focused on their sex lives, drug habits, and bad decisions, exploded in popularity. They signed a three-year deal with Barstool Sports that year.

was so popular that the duo tried to renegotiate that contract in 2020, and their friendship quickly deteriorated and became a mess of tabloid headlines and legal threats. Franklyn claimed that Cooper went behind her back and betrayed her. Cooper claimed that Franklyn was uncooperative in negotiations and deployed her boyfriend Peter Nelson (who was an HBO Sports executive at the time) to make things more difficult.

The podcast’s IP remained controlled by Barstool, and Cooper took the reins fully in May of 2020. If you look at the YouTube page, that is the beginning of history. The episodes with Franklyn, the first two years of content, are gone. Cooper has moved on. In 2021, she left Barstool and signed a $60 million contract with Spotify. In 2024, she signed a $125 million contract with Sirius XM. has evolved from a sex chat romp to one of the biggest podcasts in the world. Cooper has interviewed Kamala Harris, Michelle Obama, Kim Kardashian, and dozens of other major celebrities. The podcast, along with her persona, is softer, less raunchy, and more grown-up.

items.title: Dianna Russini’s Return To Sports Media Was A Bit Of A Disaster
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
This week marked Dianna Russini's return to public life. The former highly compensated NFL reporter, who blew up her career by canoodling in public with Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, began her return from disgrace the way a lot of notable people who can afford capable PR firms do: with a soft-focus profile in . The next phase of her comeback, Wednesday's premiere of her new weekly football show on BetUS TV, was not so competently executed.

The article is about what you'd expect. Russini talks about how "heartbreaking" the the last six months have been, and how having to resign from The Athletic after going interlaced-fingers mode with Vrabel at an adults-only resort was a "nightmare." Russini also seems to be maintaining her position that there was nothing inappropriate about her relationship with Vrabel, which included rendezvous in a bar, a casino, and on a boat. She complained to about all the "lies" that "became so out of control.” The profile finished up with Russini trying to reposition herself as an inspiration to women. “I really hope that I can be someone other women see: you can pick yourself up, get back in there and not be afraid,” she said.

With that out of the way, it was time for the main event. , a weekly one-hour web show about the NFL, debuted on Wednesday. The show is hosted by BetUS, which is a sketchy offshore sportsbook that is headquartered in Costa Rica and regulated by the government of Curaçao. items.title: An Expert And A Noob Play ‘Final Fantasy Resonance’
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
While there are many fantastic Japanese role-playing game (JRPG, for short) series out there, and with apologies to and , is the biggest and most important of them all. Every numbered entry in the main series is an event, and since almost every game is its own story (to date, there have been two main games to get direct sequels: got , and inexplicably got two sequels), there are swaths of new gamers dipping in every time a new game releases.

Despite that, it's safe to say that has somewhat lost its way, or at least what was once its identity. What started as a turn-based RPG has evolved, first into a more active-style combat system and then more recently into something bordering on an action game. This makes sense for Square Enix, the series's developer, as turn-based combat has mostly, though not entirely, slipped from an important game genre into something more niche. Chasing the action trend that took over turn-based RPG's spot with the games made financial sense, and it kept from growing stale.

That said, there's still a hunger for turn-based RPGs, and especially turn-based games; the last mainline game to be strictly turn-based was 2001's . With that in mind, we arrive at , the recently released (and relatively successful) spin-off that is a sort of remake/re-using of assets of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a mobile gacha game. is not asking the player to part with any money besides the initial price tag, and instead is a fully fleshed-out 30-to-40-hour turn-based RPG adventure through time, space, and history.

items.title: Paul George Has Turned Out To Be The Ur-Celtic
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
Get past the unseasoned beef between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in Tuesday's Celtics-Sixers matchup, and reach instead for the real juice: a killer performance by Paul George, the player for whom Brown was traded. Though a single regular-season game in November is no way useful to assess a trade in its entirety, the contrast last night between those two wings was telling: Brown (keyed-up, foul-prone, poor decision-making) sat out much of a game where George (methodical, efficient, at ease in the flow of offense) flourished. Boston won, 123-101. More than anything, George's 36-point outing was a reminder of his eerily slick, timeless style could have plugged into every NBA roster constructed over the last decade, and how it distills Joe Mazzulla's Celtics squad to its spiritual essence.

Fair minds were skeptical that a star version of George would ever return. In two years with Philly, he seemed to have receded into a fog of lower-body injuries, mystery drug use, and inconsistent podcasting, playing just 78 total regular-season games. Meanwhile, Brown had just come off a workhorse campaign for the Celtics, logging 71 games while soaking up 36 percent usage on his way to an All-NBA second team. For all the hand-wringing about Brown's true value, both in a vacuum and within the Celtics system, he was clearly the more valuable player at the time of the trade. When swapping two seemingly onerous contracts for one another, each one asking somewhere between 32 and 35 percent of the salary cap for a wing who likely wouldn't live up to that price tag, it was the Sixers who had to sweeten the deal with draft picks.

items.title: Two Hard-Up Vikings Fans “Celebrate” The Return Of Kirk Cousins
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
Three years ago, after a long but loveless marriage, the Minnesota Vikings let QB Kirk Cousins walk out the door. They felt free. Unburdened. , even. No longer would they have to spend night after night asking themselves, “Where is this relationship going?” They could finally find someone new. They could believe in love again, and maybe even have a bit of fun getting back out there on the scene.

That scene, much to the Vikings’ chagrin, turned out to be far less exciting than they’d anticipated. Maybe it was them. Maybe they weren’t quite as charming and attractive as they thought they’d been. Regardless, they eventually found themselves lonely, broken, and frankly hard up. And so, with Taylor Swift’s “Style” playing on a loop in the background, they swallowed their pride, along with a good amount of red wine, and made the call they swore they’d never make. Kirk Cousins is a Viking again, and us Vikings fans feel a little bit ashamed that we let this happen all over again. That’s the subject of this week’s special Trade Deadline Edition of All Ball.

items.title: Look Who Came Crawling Back To Kirk Cousins
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Under any other circumstances, in any other year, Kirk Cousins being traded back to the Minnesota Vikings would be universally mocked under the You Can't Make Someone Go Back Home statutes. The story of Kirk and the Vikes is one that had been told all the way through, in no great rush at that, and was on the merits not one that would have had the public demanding or even imagining a reboot. But here, now, in the situation in which the Vikings have placed themselves—well, put it this way: No NFL trade has ever had so many people call their shot ahead of time and then nod with approval after it came to pass.

Yes, even though Cousins already titillated and frustrated the Vikings alternately over six years by being Almost That Guy, they brought him back on Tuesday in a desperate admission that they had turned their quarterback room into a lividly radioactive dump site. Cousins, we must presume, went with a song in his heart, because he finally found his nirvana: a place without a young quarterback desperate to make his bones waiting to replace him.

A Cousins trade of some kind had been rumored from the moment he landed in Las Vegas to play for the Raiders, primarily because he was so obviously there to hold the place card until No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza was ready to replace him. Minnesota wasn't much of a trade option until the Vikings made themselves one—well, the only one. After Cousins was lured to Atlanta (illegally, as the league eventually ruled), the Vikings fell in and out of love with J.J. McCarthy, fell briefly in like with Kyler Murray and then watched his hamstring explode, watched Carson Wentz melt into a puddle in real time on Monday night, and rejected Max Brosmer as a viable option on the fly.

items.title: Am I Cursed To Listen To Nothing But Awful Children’s Music For The Rest Of Time?
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content: This week, Giri offers suggestions on how to avoid the pitfalls of the Toddler Music Industrial Complex.

items.title: Damian Lillard’s Second Act In Portland Is More Than Just A Nice Story
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
You'd be forgiven for briefly losing track of your place in linear time at the end of the third quarter of Tuesday night's marquee matchup between the Oklahoma City Thunder and Portland Trail Blazers. How could this be 2026, with Damian Lillard nailing a quarter-ending buzzer-beater from the logo over a cadre of defenders? Clearly we had switched tracks and were now in the realm of Dame Time, or, barring the supernatural, 2019 again.

The Blazers coasted from there for a comfy 123-103 win, in which Lillard paced his team with 25 efficient points in just 24 minutes. Every part of that sentence would have been inconceivable as recently as 18 months ago.

items.title: Nick Cousins Sure As Hell Was “Not Doing Great”
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
The Capitals beat the Senators in overtime on Tuesday, but the most impactful play of the night was not a goal. Late in the third, with the score 2-2, Ottawa's Nick Cousins kind of casually gathered the puck in his own corner and started to skate up the ice. Before he could do anything with it, however, Cousins got comprehensively bulldozed by Caps defenseman Jakob Chychrun, who sent his opponent's body into horizontal flight against the boards before it bounced limply to the ice. After a review, the refs deemed the hit clean, but Cousins did not return to action. He didn't go to the hospital, but according to his coach Travis Green, "He’s not doing great.”

I have complicated thoughts about this play. It is very difficult for me to resist marveling at Chychrun's spectacular force and its devastating aftermath; it's as real an athletic feat as any skillful dangle. The fact that it was perpetrated on Cousins, a pest so annoying that his peers named him the league's most punchable player last year, only makes it easier to ignore the human toll. But it's also hard for me to see it and not think about Claude Lemieux, among other ex-NHL tough guys, whose brain was donated to CTE research after his death by suicide earlier this year.

items.title: Bury Me At Camp Blood
items.author: Joshua Rivera
items.content:
The 2009 remake of is, by most conceivable metrics, a bad movie. Cacophonous, slapdash, and dutifully uninspired in its pursuit of tits and guts, the movie is a chore even in the forgiving eyes of horror gorehounds. But on the southwestern edge of Pennsylvania's Pocono Mountains, on the giant screen of The Mahoning Drive-In—the largest still showing movies on 35mm film—it's intoxicating. Not because of some magical idyllic drive-in experience, but for the deep, strange siren song of drive-in, and the Gathering of the Juggalos–esque events it hosts every year. There are lawn games, costume contests, and raffles. People pitch tents and set up campers, they unfold card tables and have potlucks, spread out blankets and camp chairs and spooky lamps to make it easy for friends to find them in the dark between movies. Almost everyone here is from somewhere else, and none of them care how bad the movie is. They like the movies, sure, but they love The Mahoning.

People are lured to this place. That's how most encounter it—someone brings you, serves as a guide, an evangelist. Something makes visitors want to share it with others immediately, in no small part thanks to the spectacle of events like Camp Blood, an annual celebration of slasher movies. This is my third Camp Blood; I first came here because a friend brought me, and this time I want to know how others found their way to this unremarkable patch of the Poconos. I speak to a gaggle of friends, many of which are connected by a man from New Hampshire named Keith. He united a bunch of movie fans from Boston and Ohio, and inspired them to make the long drive down to Lehighton for the Mahoning. I was eager to meet Keith, but unfortunately he was busy mainlining triple feature at another repertory house, The Gap Theatre in Wind Gap, Penn., a 48-minute drive from the triple feature that began here at sunset.

"[Keith] was like, 'The programming at this drive-in is incredible," one of the friends, a man named Desmond, tells me. "And then one year I had to go because they played , which is a dinosaur movie I'm quite fond of from the '60s … that got me out here, and it's the first drive-in I've ever been to."

items.title: Jayson Tatum And Jaylen Brown’s Beef Is Severely Undercooked
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
The weightlessness of the early season and the ever-increasing rate of injuries can make it hard to sell a weeknight NBA game in November. There remains, however, a reliable shortcut between "box score I'll check in the morning" and "game I gotta watch live," and it is a route lined with beef.

Beef was not promised in the leadup to Tuesday night's game between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which pit former teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum against each other for the first time since Brown was traded in the offseason, but a savory aroma was in the air. Brown's trade brought with it all sorts of thinly sourced reports about he and Tatum having a contentious relationship, and those suspicions were more or less confirmed a few weeks ago. On Oct. 22, Tatum posted on YouTube another episode of his self-produced documentary series. A clip of this episode, in which Tatum recounts the shock he felt when he found out that Brown had been traded—"You traded him down the street?" he says to the person who broke the news—was posted on Instagram, and in the comments section of that post, Brown responded with the "cap" emoji.

Brown was calling Tatum a liar, which was enough to elicit some direct questions about their relationship from reporters. ​"Jayson's a great guy," Brown said. "Like I said, great family, hell of a basketball player, hell of a PR team. There's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chops, and some gravy, you know what I mean? He should stay ready at all times."

items.title: What’s The Worst QB Performance You’ve Ever Seen?
items.author: Defector Staff
items.content:
In honor of Monday night's Vikings debacle, some members of the Defector staff share their memories of terrible quarterbacking.

Dan Pastorini, Oakland Raiders vs. Houston Oilers, Oct. 9, 1972

Dan Pastorini was a highly regarded but still inexperienced Houston Oiler in 1972, before any of your parents were born, and 30 years before the franchise stopped being either Houston or Oilers. But Pastorini had the bad luck of being drafted by a team that was bad and about to become much worse. He won one of his 22 starts across his second and third seasons, to give you an idea of how horrendous the Oilers were.

items.title: Institute Corporal Punishment For Democratic Strategists
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
Here is a thing that Republicans do not do when they sweep into power: They do not bother brainstorming ways that they can signal a values match with the people who oppose them, and whom they have just defeated. They do not look around, blinking, from the hilltop they have just won, and fret about appealing to the vanquished foes lying half-dead at their feet. When Republicans win, they set about changing the laws, or using the existing laws to their advantage. That is the job. Republican lawmakers express their values through the laws that they make and enforce. They do not get sidetracked by the idea that they can make friends with progressives, and not only because they know that their voters do not want them to do that. They perceive an authentic mismatch of values, and their solution to that is to make progressives eat shit.

You will say that this is a weakness of their politics. You will point to their long-dwindling popularity and last week's electoral bloodbath, and say that their reflexive and idiotic tribalism is a terminal illness, and that Democrats should learn from it only that it is self-defeating. You fool. Here you have done them the favor of flattening the actual, substantive, qualitative differences between the goals of the right and the left.

You shouldn't do that, because those differences are important. People on the left want things—actual tangible things: laws and institutions and structures—that make sense, that arise from active, curious, engaged minds thinking deeply about how to run a community of any size or complexity. Those things are aimed at the goal of making society more equitable and less brutal, and making life more dignified and less degrading.

items.title: Harrison Butker’s PAC Is Going About As Well As His Kicking
items.author: Samer Kalaf
items.content:
Harrison Butker is having the worst season of his NFL career. And if that weren't good enough news, his financial foray into politics is basically dead.

Butker, placekicker for the Kansas City Chiefs, has hit only 63.2 percent of his field goals this season. He's missed at least one field goal in six of his eight games, and his accuracy from long range has escaped him: He's 2-for-8 on field goals attempted from 50 or more yards. In Sunday's 35-12 win over the New York Jets, Butker made all five of his extra point attempts, but whiffed on a 51-yarder right before halftime. That doesn't matter much against the Jets, but against a more competitive opponent, in a game that might be decided by only three points, Butker isn't as reliable as he once was. Instead of trying to restore masculine values, he should worry more about trying to restore his mechanics.

Andy Reid remained vague on whether Butker would keep kicking for Kansas City this coming weekend. "I'll address that as we go throughout the week," the head coach said after Sunday's win. If the Chiefs were to make a change, they would likely look to the practice squad and elevate Justin Tucker, who hasn't seen NFL action since the 2024 season, and was cut by the Baltimore Ravens in 2025 after numerous massage therapists in the area accused him of sexual misconduct. K.C.'s special teams has the roster depth and moral fiber of the White House press secretary pool.

items.title: Throwing League Fits, With Lawrence Schlossman
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content: This week on , we talked about fashion. Whose style is good? Whose is bad? What exactly does a professional stylist do? Has Tyler Kolek been to Dimes Square, or is he just pretending? We got into all this and more with Lawrence Schlossman of . Lawrence knows ball and also knows clothing, so he was the ideal guy to chat with about all this stuff.

items.title: Cooper Flagg Makes It All Make Sense
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
The best players make basketball look simple. The effect is mostly illusory, a byproduct of their size and skill warping a complex game, though there's something to the idea. In essence, what a star does is make the game easier for their team and more difficult for the opponent. It's not rendering anything simple, exactly, more like adding to or subtracting from the bevy of available options for, respectively, one's team or one's opponents. You can only do simple stuff if you have the best players.

Cooper Flagg is one such player. Watching him dominate the Indiana Pacers Monday night, I was struck by how simple it all looked for the 19-year-old. With his Dallas Mavericks trailing by 10 coming out of halftime, Flagg made a point of taking and nailing three straight midrange jumpers, shots he can get to anytime he wants. Three times, the cockroach (complimentary) Pacers dodged getting squished and made their way back into one-possession range; with the game on the line, Flagg calmly got the rock and went to work.

Flagg wound up with 43 points on 25 shots in 39 minutes, 10 rebounds, six assists, and four stocks, all on the second night of a back-to-back. He played the entire fourth quarter and hit all eight of his free throws. He turns 20 next week, and is at most a few months older than the youngest draftees in the rookie class after his. He's taken to munching PB-and-Js at all times because he's still a young growing boy. Something interesting is happening in Dallas, somehow, which all comes down to Flagg's undeniable superstardom.

items.title: Jonathan Abrams Writes About NBA Players In Three Dimensions
items.author: Owen Lewis
items.content:
From 2007 to 2009, Oklahoma City Thunder general manager Sam Presti selected future NBA MVPs Kevin Durant, Russell Westbrook, and James Harden in three consecutive drafts, securing the fledgling team an otherworldly core. The results were brilliant and tumultuous. The Thunder started out 3-29 in 2008, but within a couple of years rounded into a fearsome squad that gave the 2010 Lakers a scare, and eventually reached the 2012 NBA Finals, where they went toe to toe with LeBron James's Miami Heat and lost. Then Presti traded Harden, setting in motion a future that would scatter the trio around the league. As they broke apart, they'd help mold the league into its modern shape.

Jonathan Abrams, a culture reporter who began his career covering the NBA and has written about it extensively at the , Grantland, and Bleacher Report's magazine, is out with a new book, , about these players and their importance in modern NBA history. At Grantland, Abrams wrote longform profiles and oral histories, in which you could relive the Malice at the Palace, become familiar with the particulars of how an almost-dynasty fell apart, or learn that the Orlando Magic came disturbingly close to being called the "Juice."

It's that style of dedicated reporting and patient storytelling that enlivens all three of the book's protagonists, whom Abrams refers to only by their first names. When We Were Young and Fearless leaves the reader with a fascinating image of what the 2010s Thunder could have been, but its greatest feat is perhaps the sympathy and complexity with which it imbues three of the greatest players of the 21st century.

items.title: A Brief Excursion Into The Commanders’ Idiocy
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
Time for your weekly edition of the Defector Funbag. Got something on your mind?. You can also read Drew over at. Today, we're talking about forward progress, Queens of the Stone Age, grout, and more.

I have to run a bit shorter than usual this week because I was summoned for jury duty yesterday. The juror lounge had no free coffee, and the vending machine was empty. RUDE. I was so agitated that if I had actually gotten called, I would have automatically voted to convict regardless of the evidence.

items.title: What Use Is Kevin O’Connell?
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
There are times when a team can lose a primetime game and feel hard done-by. A good squad can have an off night, or run into a particularly bad matchup, and suddenly millions of viewers have incorrectly concluded that those fellas are bad at football. The Minnesota Vikings, who came into Monday's game against the Buffalo Bills with a 6-1 record, offered no such misrepresentation. Anyone who watched that game came away with a precise understanding of who the Vikings are: a team that can't move the ball to save its life.

I shudder to think of the hypothetical casual fan who was excited to tune into a game between two six-win teams, only to be treated to a game that, despite being close in a technical sense, never really offered any drama. The Vikings are to blame for that, as they managed to lose 23-6 while putting yet another inept offensive performance on tape. Minnesota finished the game with 178 total yards and nine first downs, and possessed the ball for 17:28, their lowest mark in franchise history. That was somehow all they could manage against the 30th-ranked pass defense in the league.

The star of this horrible show was Carson Wentz, who was forced into starting quarterback duty thanks to Kyler Murray's hamstring injury. Wentz completed eight of his 25 passes for 81 yards, and threw two interceptions. It was a historically bad performance, one so vivid in its awful particulars that Joe Buck and Troy Aikman were able to set aside any hard feelings they might currently have for each other and join in channeling their disgust at the field:

items.title: The Free Press Deletes Video In Which Reporter Is Scared Of The Word “Habibi”
items.author: Brandy Jensen
items.content:
Olivia Reingold might be the most notably embarrassing employee at the Free Press, but her coworkers won't let her take that title without a fight. Last Wednesday, following the midterm elections the outlet posted a video by a different staffer who characterized Abdul El-Sayed's victory speech, which he gave almost entirely in English, as being delivered in Arabic. By Sunday, that video was deleted. The publication announced the decision, which apparently needed four days of deliberation, with the following note:

We deleted an opinion video about the use of foreign languages in election night speeches. The post contained a factual error and its tone fell short of what we believe advances healthy public discourse. The rigorous editorial process that produces the work that appears on our website and in our newsletters must apply to everything we post on social media. We’ll be updating how we do things to achieve just that. We regret the error.

The video in question was by reporter Maya Sulkin, whose accompanying caption was as follows: “Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed gave his victory speech in Arabic last night. Rep. Ilhan Omar addressed her victory party in Somali. And this morning, Iran’s supreme leader posted that America’s collapse ‘has accelerated.’ What should we make of these acceptance speeches?” The blue wave has resulted in some unlikely victories, but I didn't know that included the supreme leader of Iran.

items.title: Kings Give Up On First-Round Pick After 83 Games, Trade Him For Basically Nothing
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
Not all franchises are made equal. Some are widely understood by their peers to be operated by dullards. These imbalances are clear to everyone—fans, analysts, other executives—if not to the dullards themselves. Is it bullying whenever the Oklahoma City Thunder do business with, say, the Sacramento Kings? Maybe it is.

During the 2025 NBA Draft, these two teams kicked off the first phase of this saga. The Kings sent a top-16 protected pick belonging to the San Antonio Spurs; the Thunder sent the No. 24 pick. The Kings then used that pick to select Nique Clifford, a versatile 6-foot-5 prospect. The knock on Clifford was his age—already 23 at draft night—but he was considered a good athlete with positional size, feel, and ball skills. After a solid rookie season, he was a modest source of hope on a Sacramento roster that badly needed any. Any evaluation of Clifford would also have to factor in that he was playing under full-time head coach Doug Christie, who is the NBA franchise equivalent of swapping on the donut tire on your car and then taking it on a cross-country road trip. Christie had poor Clifford playing point guard for stretches of the season, struggling to make plays out of isolation. But at least Clifford was in no rush to prove himself, having joined a play-in franchise on a clear downward trajectory which included conducting confusing trades for middling players.

Alas, Clifford just couldn't keep up with the furious pace of innovation in Sacramento. Just 16 months after the Kings acquired him, Clifford had slipped out of the rotation. On Sunday, they traded him back to the Thunder, and in return received two-second round picks. Particularly strange is the timing of the trade. What was Sacramento's rush to move on from the sophomore? The 1-9 Kings are headed nowhere but hell. They have a lively point guard now in Darius Acuff Jr., who has been happily taking on galactic usage; their best wing, Keegan Murray, finally returned from an ankle injury yesterday. If anything, now is the time to properly test out all their rookie-scale players and assess their quality.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Admits To Affair With An Accused Spy For The Chinese Government
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
On Sunday, Nvidia announced that it was opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a Singapore-based data-center company executive named Alice Huang (no relation), whom U.S. officials say is also working as a spy for Chinese state intelligence. Given the size of Nvidia, as well as its strategic centrality to the intense AI buildout competition between the U.S. and China, Huang might be the single most desirable person in the tech industry, if not the whole world, for Beijing to honeypot. According to reporting around the matter, it seems like they got what they came for.

We must begin with the crux of the issue, which is the matter of why Nvidia is in such a central position. AI software companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have gotten significantly more media attention because they make consumer products and engage in marketing rhetoric about their potential to create the machine god, but Nvidia is the company that has made the most actual money during the ongoing AI boom. Nvidia makes chips, supposedly the best of all the chips, on which every big-time software company built its flagship platforms a few years ago. This has made Nvidia the second-biggest publicly traded company in the world, and has made its founder Jensen Huang fabulously wealthy and quite the influential figure.

It's also made the Santa Clara–based Nvidia the most critical part of the U.S. strategic plan to assert global AI dominance, by which I mean dominance over China, its principal competitor in the field. American trade policy forbids Nvidia from selling its best stuff to Chinese companies: U.S. policymakers want American companies to build the biggest and best data centers and create AI software that can most effectively and profitably book a flight for you, tell you some stuff you love about your kid, or conduct microtargeted drone assassinations of restive labor organizers.

items.title: Patriots Emit Foul Odor In Blowout Loss To Packers
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
Things have to be really bad for the New England Patriots if even Christian Gonzalez is dropping a stinker. The All-Pro cornerback has been one of the most consistent players on a Pats team that has struggled to find consistency at other positions, but Sunday against the Green Bay Packers, Gonzalez was just like many of his teammates: overwhelmed and outmatched in a 45-27 loss that was functionally over by the third quarter.

This was the worst performance of Gonzalez's pro career since he entered the NFL in 2023. Against Green Bay's receiving duo of Matthew Golden and Christian Watson, the league's highest-paid cornerback was helpless, consistently getting beat on deep routes and losing one or both in coverage for touchdowns. According to Next Gen Stats, Gonzalez gave up a total of 10 catches for 187 receiving yards on Sunday, the most of his career and the third-most of any player this season. He had given up a total of 196 receiving yards across his first six games. On Green Bay's second TD of the day, Gonzalez and teammate Marcus Jones both covered Watson as he ran to the corner, leaving Golden wide open. Late in the third quarter, Gonzalez over-leveraged toward the outside against Watson, who just ran a skinny post and essentially walked into the end zone to make the score 40-14.

"I mean, they just got the best of me today,” Gonzalez said after the loss. “I mean, this is pro football. They got good receivers like every team. So, they got the best of me today. Move on from it and be ready for next week.” His head coach Mike Vrabel was a little more pointed in his postgame comments: "When your best players don’t play good, you don’t have much of a chance in this league. So, we expect a lot more. He expects a lot more. We need more from him and everybody else."

items.title: The Bears Beat The Bucs With One Hand Tied Behind Their Backs
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
Sunday night's Bucs-Bears game possessed the major ingredients necessary for a Chicago fan freakout. Franchise quarterback Caleb Williams looked lost for much of the action, throwing four interceptions and stalling on three second-half three-and-outs. The team as a whole, meanwhile, surrendered a first-half 17-3 lead, allowing the game-tying touchdown following a fumble in the final stages of the fourth quarter. But the concerns one would have about the Bears' offense feel relatively minor today, because despite all their errors, a buzzer-beating Cairo Santos field goal and a stout defensive performance allowed Chicago to notch their fourth straight win, 27-24, improving to 7-2 as they fight for first place in the NFL's toughest division.

The first nine minutes at Soldier Field were a party. The Buccaneers, entering the game as clear underdogs but coming off their two best outings of the season, got steamrolled, allowing a pair of Williams TD passes while mustering just six yards of their own. From that point on, however, everything became a struggle. Williams chucked a pick near the end zone to conclude a drive, then tossed another on his very next chance when he tried and failed to loft the ball out of bounds to avoid a sack. Before halftime arrived, he'd gift a third pass to the defense, making a silly decision to just huck the ball forward under pressure. Watching from afar, it felt like Williams's early success had put him in a consequence-free mindset on the field, and in his postgame it did very much sound like confidence was the culprit.

"I'm going to throw until I can't throw anymore," Williams said. "That's how I live. I work my tail off to be in this position. I'll never not throw the ball. I could throw 100 picks in one game. ... That's how I grew up. That's who I am. I don't get gun-shy."

items.title: Why Wouldn’t NC State Hire Philip Rivers?
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
One imagines Philip Rivers in his fortress of solitude, away from his platoon of children and contemplating what to do with his winter now that his St. Michael Catholic High School team has been knocked out of the Alabama high school playoffs. Then it hit him: .

Of course, it didn't happen that way, because the former quarterback's name has been the one most linked with the Raleigh job since Dave Doeren got tagged and bagged in late October. The possibility of him stepping into the gig was the principal discussion point in Rivers's postgame presser after St. Michael lost to Glenwood School on Friday night. It had been considered the est of for weeks, in fact, and Rivers had already been elevated to First Candidate In Training when his son Gunner (of course that is his name), who had been Rivers's quarterback at St. Mike's, committed to NC State.

The presumption here is that Rivers's prosciutto-thin coaching résumé—in mentioning his six seasons at St. Mike, we have covered all of it—has been trumped by his ability to pry open donor pockets and make the Wolfpack relevant again in the bloated ACC. And when we say "again," we mean "as a big spender in a landscape where 'big' is $40 million a year rather than $20 million." Doeren made a point of describing the limitations that such a barebones budget played on the school's chances of being noticed, and the school responded with a simple, You're absolutely right about that, Dave-O. Now get out.

items.title: Connor Hellebuyck Won’t Start In Winnipeg Because Of “Expected Win Probability”
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Some of the most memorable nights in hockey are driven by malice. If the NHL could capture in a bottle the atmosphere of John Tavares's first trip to Long Island after signing with Toronto, or Brady Tkachuk's Ottawa return as a Panther, it could and would sell it. And fans would buy it, because what these nights are really about is catharsis: the purging of resentments and the reaffirmation of loyalties. It's a nice thing to do from time to time. Builds community. Strengthens fandom. Probably good for mental health. The crowd that boos together, cheers together.

Winnipeg wants and deserves a night of catharsis, to wish a not-so-fond farewell to Connor Hellebuyck, the greatest player the franchise has ever had, and who got so sick of both losing and living in Winnipeg that he forced his way to New Jersey. And wouldn't you know it, the Devils are on a Canada swing, and will take on the Jets on Tuesday. It ought to be personality-driven appointment viewing, in a league that doesn't have nearly enough of that. But the Devils have affirmed their commitment to non-entertainment. Connor Hellebuyck will not start in Winnipeg, per an all-timer of an official statement.

items.title: You Could Be County Clerk, Or Sheriff!
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
You—yes, you—could be in elected office today. The median Defector reader is a smart and good-looking progressive with impeccable taste. What other qualifications do you really need? Had you thrown your hat in ahead of the blue wave, today you could be your state's lieutenant governor. Hell, for that matter, maybe you your state's lieutenant governor. Have you checked your mail?

Consider the case of Sebastian Matta, a 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University. He has a 3.25 GPA, per the , and he lives at home with his parents. Starting in February, Matta will be the Superior Court Clerk of Maricopa County, which has a geographic area larger than New Jersey and a population larger than Oregon. Matta will lead a department that, according to Phoenix-area CBS affiliate KTVK, processes more than 16,000 documents per day and has an annual budget of $65 million. Matta will be the boss to some 670 veteran professional staff.

"I hope that they realize that I’m just not any 19-year-old," said Matta, hoping to give confidence to the hundreds of people who will soon be working under him in an incredibly complex bureaucracy.

items.title: The Blue Jays Have An Asshole, And His Name Is Anthony Santander
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
Outfielder Anthony Santander appears to be a brain-poisoned, red-pilled moron and an Islamophobe. On Wednesday, Santander shared to his Instagram account a video warning about America's impending adoption of Sharia law, and another about Muslims being inherently violent. The videos stayed up until Thursday, by which time they had drawn the attention of his employer, the Toronto Blue Jays. Santander then scrubbed the videos, and the Blue Jays issued a somewhat limp statement, assuring fans that "individual comments do not represent our organization's values and beliefs."

Santander seems to be getting his news from bad sources. Laura Loomer, the deranged right-wing carnival barker, told her too-many Twitter followers Tuesday night that "America is over," and falsely claimed that the midterm blue wave swept into Congress people who "openly talk about their hatred of America, love of communism, and support for Sharia law." The videos shared by Santander originated with the Instagram accounts of The American Truth Project and Nuhu Simon Jatau. The former is a right-wing propaganda dispensary whose website is littered with headlines like "300 MILLION DEAD AMERICANS" and "SATANIC PRAYER." The latter is a very obviously psychotic Nigerian man (a Lakers fan, to boot) who posts swirly-eyed videos claiming, among other things, that Muslims are pagans who worship Satan.

You don't have to be so fully submerged in Christian-right paranoia in order to encounter outright, targeted Islamophobia, and from newsmakers and publications that project a superficially convincing, far less YouTube-coded, veneer of authority. Maya Sulkin of the Free Press posted a video Wednesday (now deleted) falsely claiming that Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's senator-elect, delivered his victory speech in Arabic. Sulkin's video linked El-Sayed together with Ilhan Omar, representative from Minnesota, and Aber Kawas, a newly elected state senator from New York, to make the explicit case that America is under attack from, uhh, democratically elected American Muslims. "I wonder if this sounds like America to you," ponders Sulkin, twitching and quivering with panic. It was not until late Friday afternoon that the Free Press got around to dumping a correction onto Twitter, acknowledging that El-Sayed's speech was delivered in English, with three Arabic phrases thrown in. "The Free Press regrets the error," claimed the Free Press, falsely.

items.title: Caleb Williams Is Carrying All Of Chicago Sports On His Back
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Caleb Williams is carrying an unimaginable burden, and it's not just the matter of being the last living quarterback in the NFL, or easing into his place as the best Chicago Bears quarterback in three quarters of a century while running the most prolific Bears offense in 50 years. It's been only eight weeks since his season began, and already he is the preeminent face of Chicago sports. This looks like high praise, but while that praise would be deserved where Williams is concerned, consider the context.

Williams is not working against a deep field—not in the NFC North, which is the toughest division in the league, but in the town in which he works. There, his opposition is Northwestern's football team, which is 6-2 but unranked and unlikely to break through the upper crust of the Big Ten. The Cubs were routed from the postseason in the shortest possible amount of time, and the White Sox are still striking out despite their season having ended four weeks ago. The Sky are notable only for having turned Angel Reese into a useful player by trading her to another team. And the Bulls and Blackhawks are demonstrably god-awful, well within the margin for error for having a spectacular margin for errors. You know, like the post-election Republican mood.

How god-awful, you ask, since you've been averting your eyes? The Bulls are 1-7, and are losing their games by an average of 18 points per game, which ranks as the largest margin of stinkage in NBA history, albeit in this admittedly minuscule sample; they are allowing the second-highest number of points per game ever. They will doubtless revert to a gentler if still depressing mean, as all non-expansion teams tend to do, but with a starting lineup of Caleb Wilson, Norman Powell, Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis, and Jalen Smith, it would be foolish to rule out the 11-71 outcome for their season.

items.title: Florida State Stares Into The Abyss
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Mike Norvell is finally, officially out of my life. I am ecstatic, but I am also left completely cold. The good thing about having a hatable figure looming large over your school is that they absorb all the problems that exist, in that program and everywhere else. My opinion about his coaching is a matter of public record, but I'll say this: Norvell and that dumb face of his made for a good lightning rod, all things considered.

But now he's gone. Athletic director Michael Alford was gone in September. Thanks to an approximately $50 million buyout for Norvell and the general changing landscape of college football, the future of FSU football is more uncertain than it has ever been.

items.title: Farewell To The Cybertruck, A Total Failure
items.author: Albert Burneko
items.content:
The Tesla car company "will be winding down production of the Cybertruck" in 2027, according to a tweet from Elon Musk. Like everything else Musk says, ever, this must be treated as having essentially no truth value whatsoever and at best a coincidental relationship to anything that later happens with or to Cybertruck production. It's noteworthy as an index of what Musk wants people to believe—it's noteworthy, then, that Musk wants people to believe that the era of Cybertruck production is coming to an end.

And by "noteworthy," I mean: fucking hilarious!

Few vehicles live on in history as metonyms for failure and embarrassment. Edsel, DeLorean, whatever poor beleaguered machine ferries the Sacramento Kings to a given road game instead of doing them the favor of exploding along the way. Add to these the Cybertruck, one of the most hyped vehicles of all time; Tesla's production capacity for the Cybertruck reportedly was something like 250,000 units , and, should the end of its production in fact come in 2027, it will wrap up its four-year run certainly having sold, in total, worldwide, under half of that number. Given the ballooning demand for electric vehicles, the relative lack of competition among all-electric trucks, Tesla's huge head-start in EV production, the unparalleled hype around the Cybertruck's release, and its flowering into a rolling emblem of Musk's personal toxicity, the Cybertruck deserves to endure in history as among the most embarrassing mass-produced products ever available for purchase by human beings. I'd rather carry a battery-powered Big Mouth Billy Bass around under my arm for a year than be seen, by any single person, climbing into or out of a Cybertruck once.

items.title: Now We Know How Much Money Bill Simmons Had His Daughter’s Boyfriend Bet For Him
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
Bill Simmons got himself into some trouble a few weeks ago, when he admitted on his podcast that he had engaged in proxy betting. Simmons, who lives in California, where online sports gambling is still illegal, told his listeners that he had instructed his daughter's boyfriend, who lives in gambling-friendly Massachusetts, to log into his FanDuel account and place bets on his behalf. Because this practice is strictly prohibited by FanDuel's policies, his bets were voided. But a question remained: How much action was Simmons denied?

Now, thanks to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission, we have an answer to that question. Sports betting reporter Geoff Zochodne pointed out that the commission's Investigation and Enforcement Bureau made a presentation to commissioners Thursday about Simmons's infraction. A memo announcing the presentation provided some details about how much Simmons was trying to bet:

The incident involved an admission made by media personality Bill Simmons on his August 30, 2026, podcast pertaining to his placement of proxy wagers on his FanDuel account in Massachusetts through an acquaintance who was physically present in Massachusetts. FanDuel reported that the matter involved 22 wagers with a total handle of $21,800 placed over three (3) dates: August 5, 2026, August 7, 2026, and August 19, 2026.

items.title: That’ll About Do It For The Joe Fagnano Experience
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Plenty of teams have lost their starting quarterbacks, to things like knee surgery (Giants), blood clots (Eagles), or an ancient Hittite curse (Chargers). But it's unlikely that anyone's had a rougher go of it under center this year than the Baltimore Ravens. Already sliding out of the ranks of the contenders, Baltimore was without Lamar Jackson for three punchless games due to an ankle sprain, and then, last weekend, he tore up his thumb on his very first snap in his return. His replacement Snoop Huntley is presentable as far as QB2s go, having been here on and off since 2020; Huntley was then promptly injured in the second quarter, and is out for the season with turf toe.

Just about any NFL team is dead meat after the loss of two quarterbacks, but the Ravens are extra-pungent carrion. Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie out of Maine and UConn who walked on and played seven years in college, was the sacrificial lamb for Thursday night's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. And while I have plenty of sympathy for Fagnano and the Ravens offense for only having a short week to prepare, this was indeed Thursday-ass football.

items.title: More States Banned Trans Kids From Sports This Week
items.author: Diana Moskovitz
items.content:
Four different states put forward ballot measures on Tuesday that, if passed, would either strengthen or create new laws keeping trans children out of school sports. Though the night saw massive Democratic victories, even in typical Republican strongholds like Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina, the four initiatives on the ballot tell a different story.

In two states, Arizona and Nebraska, the language will strengthen bans that were already on the books. In the other two states, Washington and Colorado, voters were asked to create new bans where none existed. As of Thursday, ballot measures in Arizona, Nebraska, and Washington were all projected to pass. Colorado's was too close to call, but the numbers leaned toward passage. Per TransAthlete.com, the passage of all four would bring the number of bans in the country, through either law or policy, up to 31.

items.title: Free Press Dumbass Has An AI Whoopsie
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
Anyone familiar with the Free Press, and its institutional project of dehumanizing Arabs, would have known that Abdul El-Sayed's U.S. Senate election win was going to have a bad effect on some of its employees. Indeed, staff writer Olivia Reingold and reporter Maya Sulkin are currently competing to see who can crash out the hardest. Whereas Sulkin has taken the obvious route of recording herself quivering in fear at the sound of El-Sayed's name and his use of a few Arabic words, Reingold opted for something more perplexing: using artificial intelligence to produce an uncanny image of a woman's feet.

"So far at Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event I’ve spotted, Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items," Reingold wrote on Tuesday night. She attached this photo to her message:

items.title: Broadcast This Wemby Performance Into Space
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
In 1974, scientists sent into space a radio message encoding some basic facts about Earth and humanity. In the "Arecibo message," we shared with the cosmos some information about the shape and size of human beings, and the composition of human DNA. This year, we should run it back, but with the following video message instead. Any life form out there should know that they are welcome here after receiving this:

Victor Wembanyama logged 52 points, 24 rebounds, and eight blocks in the San Antonio Spurs' thrilling 112-111 win over the Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday. It was a totalizing, two-way performance. Almost every possession offered a jump scare, as Wembanyama moved through space in ways heretofore unseen, or fused size and skill in ways not thought possible. Shots that would never been at risk of being blocked, at any previous point in NBA history, were in fact blocked. The 7-foot-4 guy blocking them was also beating his defender from the perimeter with a hesitation dribble. No one else mattered.
